y-m-14-01.title: Do triangles with different shapes have the same area? Comparing three triangles
y-m-14-01.topic: Area of a triangle: triangles with the same base and height
y-m-14-01.goal: Judge, giving reasons, that triangles have the same area when their bases and heights are equal even if the vertices are in different places, and handle the case where the height falls outside the base in the same way.
y-m-14-01.material: On grid paper, you drew a horizontal line and, on it, a segment ㄱㄴ (the base) that is 6 cm long. Then you drew a second horizontal line parallel to the first, 4 cm above it. On the upper line you marked points ㄷ, ㄹ, and ㅁ. Point ㄷ is directly above ㄱ. Point ㄹ is directly above the midpoint of segment ㄱㄴ. Point ㅁ is directly above a spot 2 cm to the right of ㄴ (outside segment ㄱㄴ). You joined each of ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ to ㄱ and ㄴ to make triangles ㄱㄴㄷ, ㄱㄴㄹ, and ㄱㄴㅁ. There is no picture, so draw it in words. ㄱㄴㄷ is a right triangle, ㄱㄴㄹ is a triangle with a pointed top, and ㄱㄴㅁ is a triangle that lies stretched out sideways.
y-m-14-01.thinking.0: Telling a judgment made by eye from a judgment with reasons
y-m-14-01.thinking.1: Finding the quantities needed for the comparison (base, height) in the given information
y-m-14-01.thinking.2: Checking a misconception ('the height must be inside the triangle')
y-m-14-01.prereq.0: Knowing the meaning of the base and height of a triangle
y-m-14-01.prereq.1: Reading the distance between two parallel lines on grid paper
y-m-14-01.s.s1.prompt: By eye, triangle ㄱㄴㄹ looks the largest. How will you decide by comparing the areas of the three triangles?
y-m-14-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write down separately what is the same and what is different among the three triangles.
y-m-14-01.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the lengths measured straight down from vertices ㄷ, ㄹ, and ㅁ to the lower line.
y-m-14-01.s.s1.o.a: Triangle ㄱㄴㄹ has the largest area. Its pointed top is right in the middle.
y-m-14-01.s.s1.r.a: This judgment was made from how the triangles look. Think about what decides the area, and first compare the base and height in this information.
y-m-14-01.s.s1.o.b: Triangle ㄱㄴㅁ has the largest area. It stretches out the farthest to the side.
y-m-14-01.s.s1.r.b: You may have taken how spread out it looks as its area. The length it stretches sideways and the area are different quantities.
y-m-14-01.s.s1.o.c: All three triangles have base 6 cm and height 4 cm, so their areas are the same.
y-m-14-01.s.s1.r.c: This choice was made by finding the base and height and comparing them.
y-m-14-01.s.s1.o.d: The shapes are different, so the areas are different too, and you have to calculate to know which is larger.
y-m-14-01.s.s1.r.d: Wanting to calculate is a good attitude. However, 'different shapes mean different areas' is not a confirmed fact; it is an idea to be tested.
y-m-14-01.s.s1.explain: The three triangles have the same base ㄱㄴ (6 cm), and all three vertices lie on the same line parallel to the base, so the height is the same, 4 cm. No matter where the vertex is, the distance between two parallel lines does not change, so the areas of all three triangles are the same: 6×4÷2=12 cm².
y-m-14-01.s.s2.prompt: Jiho explained triangle ㄱㄴㅁ as below. Pick the first line that goes wrong.
y-m-14-01.s.s2.hint.0: Check whether Jiho's claim that 'the height cannot be measured' is right by drawing a perpendicular from point ㅁ down to the lower line.
y-m-14-01.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether the length changes when the height is measured at a spot on the extended base line rather than on base ㄱㄴ itself.
y-m-14-01.s.s2.line.0: The base of triangle ㄱㄴㅁ is segment ㄱㄴ, and it is 6 cm.
y-m-14-01.s.s2.line.1: Point ㅁ is outside base ㄱㄴ, so a height cannot be measured straight down from the vertex to the base.
y-m-14-01.s.s2.line.2: So triangle ㄱㄴㅁ has no height, and its area cannot be found.
y-m-14-01.s.s2.line.3: Therefore triangle ㄱㄴㅁ cannot be compared with the other two triangles in area.
y-m-14-01.s.s2.explain: It goes wrong at line 2. The height is the length measured perpendicularly from the vertex to the base (or to the base extended). Even though point ㅁ is outside the base, the upper line is parallel to the base, so the height is still 4 cm. So the conclusions in lines 3 and 4 do not hold either, and the area of triangle ㄱㄴㅁ is also 6×4÷2=12 cm².
y-m-14-01.s.s3.prompt: Explain your judgment about the areas of the three triangles using numbers, so that a friend who cannot see the grid paper can understand.
y-m-14-01.s.s3.hint.0: First write down what length the three triangles have in common.
y-m-14-01.s.s3.hint.1: Add one line on why that length is also the same for a vertex outside the base, like point ㅁ.
y-m-14-01.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. The three triangles have base ... and height ...
y-m-14-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation include both 'the bases are the same' and 'the heights are the same'?
y-m-14-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write how you looked at the height when point ㅁ is outside the base?
y-m-14-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you use numbers (6, 4, 12, etc.) that support your judgment?
y-m-14-01.s.s3.model.0: The three triangles have the same base, 6 cm, and all the vertices lie on the same line parallel to the base, so the height is also the same, 4 cm. So the areas are all the same: 6×4÷2=12 cm².
y-m-14-01.s.s3.model.1: Even if you move the vertex along the upper line, the distance to the base does not change. Even if point ㅁ is outside the base, the height is 4 cm. So triangles with base 6 cm and height 4 cm have the same area, 12 cm², even if their shapes are different.
y-m-14-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: There is no calculation, but the reason for being the same was explained in words.

y-m-14-02.title: What do we need to know to determine the area of the paper for one kite?
y-m-14-02.topic: Area of a rhombus: the information needed to determine the area
y-m-14-02.goal: Sort out which information is enough and which is not enough to determine the area of a rhombus, design different rhombuses with the same area, and explain why the side length alone does not determine the area.
y-m-14-02.material: A workshop makes paper kites in the shape of a rhombus. A rhombus is a quadrilateral whose four sides are all the same length. Each kite comes with different information, and we want to work out whether that information alone determines, as one value, the area of the paper used to make one kite. All lengths are in cm, and a kite is thought of as one flat sheet of paper. The pieces of information below are about different kites.
y-m-14-02.thinking.1: Imagining what varies in many ways because of missing information
y-m-14-02.thinking.2: Making different solutions with the same area
y-m-14-02.prereq.0: Knowing that a rhombus is a quadrilateral whose four sides are all the same length
y-m-14-02.prereq.1: Knowing the diagonals of a rhombus and the base and height of a parallelogram
y-m-14-02.s.s1.prompt: From the information below, choose all the items for which knowing that one piece of information alone lets you determine the area of the kite's paper as one value.
y-m-14-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each piece of information, check whether you can think of a rhombus that satisfies it exactly but has a different area.
y-m-14-02.s.s1.hint.1: Take a rhombus frame made by joining four sticks and press it flat from one side. See what changes and what stays the same.
y-m-14-02.s.s1.o.a: All four sides are 30 cm, and so the perimeter is 120 cm
y-m-14-02.s.s1.r.a: Even if the side lengths are the same, the area changes when the rhombus is pressed flat or stood up. The side length does not fix how much it leans.
y-m-14-02.s.s1.o.b: One side is 20 cm, and the height to that side is 18 cm
y-m-14-02.s.s1.r.b: This is the idea of seeing the rhombus as a parallelogram with a base and a height, so its area can be determined.
y-m-14-02.s.s1.o.c: The length of one diagonal is 40 cm
y-m-14-02.s.s1.r.c: Even if one diagonal is the same, the area changes if the other diagonal gets longer or shorter.
y-m-14-02.s.s1.o.d: The lengths of the two diagonals are 40 cm and 24 cm
y-m-14-02.s.s1.r.d: This is the idea that the lengths of the two diagonals fix the size and shape of the rhombus.
y-m-14-02.s.s1.o.e: The size of one angle is 60°
y-m-14-02.s.s1.r.e: The size of an angle fixes only the leaning shape, not the size (length). There are as many rhombuses of different sizes as you like.
y-m-14-02.s.s1.explain: To determine the area, you need to know the size and the shape together. The two diagonals (40×24÷2=480 cm²) or one side and the height to that side (20×18=360 cm²) fix the area as one value. With the four side lengths alone, one diagonal alone, or one angle alone, the area can come out in many ways.
y-m-14-02.s.s2.prompt: You are designing a kite shaped like a rhombus with an area of 240 cm². Choose the lengths a and b of the two diagonals (natural numbers, each at least 10 cm and at most 60 cm) and make 3 different kites. (Swapping the two diagonals counts as the same kite.)
y-m-14-02.s.s2.hint.0: Choose the length of one diagonal first, then fit the other diagonal so that the area is 240 cm².
y-m-14-02.s.s2.hint.1: If a value is not a natural number from 10 cm to 60 cm, change the first diagonal and try again.
y-m-14-02.s.s2.ok.c1: Both diagonals are natural numbers from 10 cm to 60 cm.
y-m-14-02.s.s2.fail.c1: The diagonals must be natural numbers (in cm) from 10 cm to 60 cm.
y-m-14-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The area is not 240 cm². Check the area again using the lengths of the two diagonals.
y-m-14-02.s.s2.explain: The kites that satisfy the conditions are the five (10, 48), (12, 40), (15, 32), (16, 30), and (20, 24) (swapping the two diagonals gives the same kite). Even with the same area, the kites look different from one another.
y-m-14-02.s.s3.prompt: A friend said, 'Rhombuses whose four sides are all 30 cm all have the same area.' Decide whether this is right, and write what else you would need to know to decide.
y-m-14-02.s.s3.hint.0: Picture two rhombuses whose four sides are all 30 cm, and draw one close to a square and one flattened.
y-m-14-02.s.s3.hint.1: Write down what lengths you would need to be told in order to compare those two rhombuses.
y-m-14-02.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. No, because ... So what we need to know more is ...
y-m-14-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your judgment include the reason 'even if the sides are the same, the shape can differ'?
y-m-14-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write at least one specific piece of information that you would need to know more?
y-m-14-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you connect it with the earlier steps of this task, checking whether that information would really fix the area as one value?
y-m-14-02.s.s3.model.0: No. Even if all the sides are 30 cm, the area can change if you press it flat. You have to be told the lengths of the two diagonals or the height to know the area.
y-m-14-02.s.s3.model.1: You can't tell from the side length alone. If you are told the height when one side is 30 cm, or the lengths of the two diagonals, then it is fixed.
y-m-14-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: Without flatly saying 'no', I said that it can't be known and what information is needed.

y-m-14-03.title: Can we trust the formula used to find the area of a trapezoid?
y-m-14-03.topic: Area of a trapezoid: testing a formula
y-m-14-03.goal: Explain how to test whether a formula for an area is wrong, using special cases (a rectangle, a triangle) or an estimate (an enclosing rectangle), and how to interpret that test correctly.
y-m-14-03.material: There is a flower bed shaped like a trapezoid. Two sides are parallel; the top side is 4 m and the bottom side is 10 m. The distance (height) between the two parallel sides is 4 m. Raon said the area of this flower bed is (top side + bottom side)×height = (4+10)×4 = 56 m². The classmates are talking about ways to find out whether Raon's formula is right.
y-m-14-03.thinking.0: Testing with a special case before trusting a formula
y-m-14-03.thinking.1: Estimating whether the size of an answer makes sense
y-m-14-03.thinking.2: Questioning whether one example guarantees every case
y-m-14-03.prereq.0: Knowing the top side, bottom side, and height of a trapezoid
y-m-14-03.prereq.1: Knowing the areas of a rectangle and a triangle
y-m-14-03.s.s1.prompt: If Raon's formula (top side + bottom side)×height were wrong, which tests could reveal that fact? Choose all that are appropriate.
y-m-14-03.s.s1.hint.0: If the formula is right, then even when used on an easy shape it must give the area we already know. Think of a shape whose area you know.
y-m-14-03.s.s1.hint.1: Draw an easy shape that can completely contain the flower bed, and think about which can be larger, the area of the flower bed or the area of that shape.
y-m-14-03.s.s1.o.a: Count how many friends answered 56 m², and treat the most common answer as right
y-m-14-03.s.s1.r.a: Many people giving the same answer is not evidence that the formula is right.
y-m-14-03.s.s1.o.b: Compare the value from this formula with the real area when the top and bottom sides are equal (a rectangle)
y-m-14-03.s.s1.r.b: This is the idea of testing by comparing the result of the formula with the area of a shape you already know.
y-m-14-03.s.s1.o.c: Put the same numbers into the same formula and calculate once more, to see whether 56 comes out again and check there is no calculation mistake
y-m-14-03.s.s1.r.c: Repeating the same calculation reduces calculation mistakes, but it does not test whether the formula itself is right.
y-m-14-03.s.s1.o.d: Compare 56 m² with the area of the enclosing rectangle that is 10 m wide and 4 m tall
y-m-14-03.s.s1.r.d: This is the idea of testing by estimate whether the answer is a size that could fit inside the shape.
y-m-14-03.s.s1.o.e: Shrink the top side to 0 m so that it becomes a triangle, and compare the value from this formula with the real area of the triangle
y-m-14-03.s.s1.r.e: This is the idea of turning the shape into a special case and comparing the result of the formula with a known area.
y-m-14-03.s.s1.explain: A formula that may be wrong can be tested by comparing with cases where the answer is already known. Examples are a rectangle (with 10 m and 4 m, the formula gives 80 m² but the real area is 40 m²), an enclosing rectangle (10×4=40 m², so 56 m² is larger and makes no sense), and a triangle (the formula gives 10×4=40 m² but the real area is 20 m²). The number of people who gave an answer, or repeating the same calculation, is not evidence that the formula is right.
y-m-14-03.s.s2.prompt: Eunseo wrote up the test with the top side set to 0 m as below. Pick the first line that goes wrong.
y-m-14-03.s.s2.hint.0: Check whether the area of the triangle Eunseo used in line 3 is right, by fitting the triangle inside a rectangle with the same height and comparing.
y-m-14-03.s.s2.hint.1: Look at how many triangles you get when you cut a rectangle along one diagonal.
y-m-14-03.s.s2.line.0: If the top side is 0 m, the trapezoid becomes a triangle.
y-m-14-03.s.s2.line.1: Then Raon's formula becomes (0+bottom side)×height, that is, bottom side×height.
y-m-14-03.s.s2.line.2: The area of a triangle is also base×height, so the two values are the same.
y-m-14-03.s.s2.line.3: Therefore Raon's formula is right for a triangle, and we can say it is right for a trapezoid too.
y-m-14-03.s.s2.explain: Line 3 goes wrong. The area of a triangle is not base×height but base×height÷2. Then, when the top side is set to 0, Raon's formula gives twice the real area, so this test shows that Raon's formula is wrong. And as in line 4, being right in one or two cases does not mean it is right in every case.
y-m-14-03.s.s3.prompt: Write to Raon: choose one test that shows Raon's formula is wrong, write its result, and also write how to fix the formula.
y-m-14-03.s.s3.hint.0: Decide on one shape to test, and first write down its real area.
y-m-14-03.s.s3.hint.1: For that shape, compare the value from Raon's formula with the real area.
y-m-14-03.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. If we use it on a rectangle ... So ...
y-m-14-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In the test you chose, did you compare the value from the formula with the real area using numbers?
y-m-14-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why that difference is evidence that Raon's formula is wrong?
y-m-14-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check whether your corrected formula gives 28 m² for Raon's flower bed?
y-m-14-03.s.s3.model.0: If we use Raon's formula on a rectangle whose top and bottom sides are equal, for example 10 m wide and 4 m tall, we get (10+10)×4=80 m², but the real area is 40 m². It comes out double, so we should divide by 2 and fix it to (top side + bottom side)×height÷2.
y-m-14-03.s.s3.model.1: The enclosing rectangle that is 10 m wide and 4 m tall has an area of 40 m², but Raon's answer of 56 m² is bigger than that, which makes no sense. Half of 56, 28 m², is right, and the formula should be fixed to (4+10)×4÷2.
y-m-14-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: I used the enclosing rectangle as the test and even recalculated with the corrected formula.

y-m-14-04.title: What do we need to know to draw the same triangle?
y-m-14-04.topic: Congruent triangles: conditions that determine one triangle
y-m-14-04.goal: As information is given one piece at a time, revise your judgment about whether a congruent triangle is determined as one triangle, and make a counterexample showing the same method does not work for quadrilaterals.
y-m-14-04.material: Seoa drew triangle ㄱㄴㄷ on paper. Her friend Minho has to draw a triangle that fits exactly on top of (is congruent to) Seoa's triangle. Seoa tells him the information about the triangle one piece at a time. Lengths are in cm, and the size of an angle is given in degrees (°).
y-m-14-04.thinking.0: Changing your judgment and confidence as information increases
y-m-14-04.thinking.1: Telling whether information fixes only the shape or also the size
y-m-14-04.thinking.2: Checking a generalization with a counterexample
y-m-14-04.prereq.0: The meaning of congruence (same shape and size, so they fit exactly on top of each other)
y-m-14-04.prereq.1: The sides and angles of a triangle; drawing triangles with a ruler and protractor
y-m-14-04.s.s1.prompt: Each time you receive information from Seoa, predict whether a congruent triangle is determined as one triangle, and revise your judgment.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.hint.0: Each time you receive information, imagine whether you can draw two triangles of different sizes that both satisfy that information.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.hint.1: For information 2, first draw the 7 cm side, then draw the angles at both ends and follow where the two lines meet.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.0.info: Information 1: The three angles of triangle ㄱㄴㄷ are: angle ㄱ is 40°, angle ㄴ is 60°, and angle ㄷ is 80°.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: With only this information, can you draw one triangle that fits exactly on top of Seoa's triangle?
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.0.after: Even if the angles are the same, there are triangles of different sizes (drawn larger or smaller). Angles tell how much the shape leans, but they do not tell the size. You need more information that fixes the size.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: You can. If the three angles are the same, then not only the shape but also the size becomes exactly the same.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You took the angles being the same to mean the size is the same too. Angles only tell how much it leans.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is not determined as one. Even with the same angles, you can draw triangles of different sizes.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This choice was made by thinking of triangles with the same angles and different sizes.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: We can't tell right now. We have to change the size and draw it ourselves to know.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This choice first thought of a way to check a guess.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Information 2: The length of side ㄴㄷ, which has angle ㄴ (60°) and angle ㄷ (80°) at its two ends, is 7 cm.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: This information has been added to information 1. Now is a triangle that fits exactly on top of Seoa's triangle determined as one?
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.1.after: If you draw the 7 cm side ㄴㄷ and then draw 60° and 80° at its two ends, the two lines meet at one point ㄱ, and the triangle is determined as one. With angles alone you did not know the size, but one side fixes the size.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It is still not determined as one. With the length of just one side, the lengths of the other two sides can vary in many ways.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This judgment did not look at how that side and the angles are tied together, even though one side is known.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It is determined as one. If you draw 60° and 80° at the two ends of the 7 cm side, the remaining point is fixed in one place.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This judgment used the fact that the side and angles are connected to each other.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: We can't judge whether it is determined, because we don't know between which angles side ㄴㄷ lies.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You missed the position already written in the information. Read again what the angles at the two ends of side ㄴㄷ are.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.2.info: Information 3: This time, for a different triangle ㅁㅂㅅ, only the lengths of two sides are given. Side ㅁㅂ is 7 cm and side ㅂㅅ is 5 cm, and the angles and the length of the remaining side are not known.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: If you were told just one more thing so that triangle ㅁㅂㅅ is determined as one, which information would help? (Choose the ones that help.)
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.2.after: The lengths of two sides alone do not determine a triangle. If you are given the angle between the two sides or the length of the remaining side, it is determined. Information that only gives a name, such as isosceles triangle or acute triangle, narrows the possibilities but does not determine one triangle.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The size of angle ㅁㅂㅅ, the angle between side ㅁㅂ and side ㅂㅅ
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This choice was made by thinking that the angle between the sides fixes how far apart the two sides open.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: That triangle ㅁㅂㅅ is an isosceles triangle (a triangle with two sides of equal length)
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: If it is isosceles, the remaining side can be 7 cm or 5 cm, two possibilities, so it is still not determined as one.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The length of the remaining side ㅁㅅ
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This choice was made by thinking that if all three side lengths are given, the triangle is determined.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: That triangle ㅁㅂㅅ is an acute triangle (a triangle whose three angles are all smaller than a right angle)
y-m-14-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: With only the information that all three angles are smaller than a right angle, the length of the remaining side can come out in many ways.
y-m-14-04.s.s1.reflect: Look at how your judgment changed in going from information 1 to information 2. At first it is easy to believe that angles alone are enough. But angles fix only the shape, while lengths fix the size too. If, each time information increases, you ask 'what could still be many things?', you can tell the reasons to change your judgment from the reasons to keep it.
y-m-14-04.s.s2.prompt: Haram said, 'Any two quadrilaterals whose four side lengths are all 5 cm are always congruent.' Decide whether this is right, and explain the reason or give an example.
y-m-14-04.s.s2.hint.0: Draw one quadrilateral whose four sides are all 5 cm, then hold one vertex and push it sideways to change the shape.
y-m-14-04.s.s2.hint.1: Look at whether the quadrilateral before pushing and the one after pushing would fit exactly on top of each other.
y-m-14-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: In the example you gave, is it clear why the two quadrilaterals do not fit on top of each other even though the four sides are the same?
y-m-14-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say that, unlike a triangle, the shape of a quadrilateral is not fixed by its side lengths alone?
y-m-14-04.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you know and write that one example is enough to break the word 'always'?
y-m-14-04.s.s2.model.0: No. Even if all four sides are 5 cm, a square and the rhombus made by pressing that square sideways have different angle sizes, so they are not congruent. The shape of a quadrilateral is not fixed by the side lengths alone.
y-m-14-04.s.s2.model.1: They may not be congruent. If you push the top of a square with four sides of 5 cm sideways and tilt it, the side lengths stay the same but the shape changes, so it does not fit on top of the first quadrilateral.
y-m-14-04.s.s2.modelNote.1: I explained in words the process of pushing and tilting the square.

y-m-14-05.title: Is 'if it is line symmetric, it is point symmetric' true? Testing with a counterexample
y-m-14-05.goal: Test, by folding and by turning, whether a generalization about line-symmetric and point-symmetric figures (the second statement) always holds, and give and explain a counterexample yourself.
y-m-14-05.material: Haram said, “If a figure is line symmetric, it is also point symmetric.” A line-symmetric figure is a figure that fits exactly onto itself when folded along a line, and a point-symmetric figure is a figure that fits exactly onto the original figure when turned half a turn (180°) around a point. There are no pictures, so think of the figures by their names. Think of the rectangle as one that is not a square, and the parallelogram as one that is neither a rectangle nor a rhombus.
y-m-14-05.thinking.0: Testing a generalization with a counterexample
y-m-14-05.thinking.1: Telling apart the two ways of checking, folding and turning half a turn
y-m-14-05.thinking.2: Making your own counterexample for a statement that does not hold
y-m-14-05.prereq.0: Line-symmetric figure: a figure that fits exactly onto itself when folded along a line
y-m-14-05.prereq.1: Point-symmetric figure: a figure that fits exactly onto the original figure when turned half a turn (180°) around a point
y-m-14-05.s.s1.prompt: Among the figures below, choose all the figures that show Haram's statement 'if a figure is line symmetric, it is also point symmetric' is not true.
y-m-14-05.s.s1.hint.0: For each figure, write in a two-column table 'Is there a line you can fold along so it fits?' and 'Does it fit when turned half a turn?'
y-m-14-05.s.s1.hint.1: Say which combination of boxes in the table you need in order to break Haram's statement.
y-m-14-05.s.s1.r.a: This choice checked both whether it fits when folded and whether it fits when turned half a turn.
y-m-14-05.s.s1.r.b: A rectangle fits both when folded and when turned, so it does not contradict Haram's statement. To show the statement is wrong, you need a figure that is line symmetric but not point symmetric.
y-m-14-05.s.s1.r.c: A parallelogram has no line you can fold along so it fits. To test Haram's statement, the figure must first be line symmetric.
y-m-14-05.s.s1.r.d: This choice checked both the line that makes it fit when folded and whether it fits when turned.
y-m-14-05.s.s1.r.e: A rhombus fits both when folded and when turned, so it does not contradict Haram's statement.
y-m-14-05.s.s1.explain: A counterexample is a figure that is 'line symmetric but not point symmetric'. The equilateral triangle and the regular pentagon have lines along which they fit when folded, but they do not fit the original shape when turned half a turn. The rectangle and the rhombus fit both ways, and the parallelogram is point symmetric but not line symmetric, so it cannot be a counterexample to this statement.
y-m-14-05.s.s2.prompt: This time Haram said the opposite. “If a figure is point symmetric, it is also line symmetric.” A parallelogram that is neither a rectangle nor a rhombus fits the original figure when turned half a turn around a point. How can you judge Haram's second statement using this parallelogram?
y-m-14-05.s.s2.hint.0: Try cutting a parallelogram out of paper and see whether there is a way to fold it so that both sides fit.
y-m-14-05.s.s2.hint.1: Think about how many examples you need to break the word 'always'.
y-m-14-05.s.s2.o.a: A parallelogram is a point-symmetric figure, so it is an example showing Haram's second statement is right.
y-m-14-05.s.s2.r.a: You only checked that it is point symmetric and did not check whether it is line symmetric. For the statement to be right, it must also be line symmetric.
y-m-14-05.s.s2.o.b: If a parallelogram has no line along which it fits when folded, this one figure is enough to say the statement is wrong.
y-m-14-05.s.s2.r.b: This judgment connects the way of checking with the conclusion.
y-m-14-05.s.s2.o.c: One figure is not enough to say the statement is wrong, so we can decide only after looking at a few more figures.
y-m-14-05.s.s2.r.c: You missed that the word 'always' can be broken by even one example.
y-m-14-05.s.s2.o.d: Folding to see whether it fits and turning to see whether it fits are the same check, so you only need to try one.
y-m-14-05.s.s2.r.d: The two checks look at different properties. Some figures have only one of them.
y-m-14-05.s.s2.explain: For 'if a figure is point symmetric, it is line symmetric' to be always right, every point-symmetric figure would also have to have a line along which it fits when folded. A parallelogram that is neither a rectangle nor a rhombus has no line along which it fits when folded, so it is a counterexample that is point symmetric but not line symmetric. One counterexample is enough to break 'always'.
y-m-14-05.s.s3.prompt: Give one figure that is line symmetric but not point symmetric, other than the equilateral triangle and the regular pentagon. Write both how it looks when folded and how it looks when turned half a turn, and explain why that figure is a counterexample to Haram's first statement.
y-m-14-05.s.s3.hint.0: Decide on a figure, and first write where you can draw the line along which it fits when folded.
y-m-14-05.s.s3.hint.1: Follow where the part that was on top goes when you turn that figure half a turn.
y-m-14-05.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. An isosceles triangle, when folded, ... When turned half a turn, ...
y-m-14-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say where the line is, to show that the figure you gave really fits when folded?
y-m-14-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write why it does not fit the original shape when turned half a turn (which part goes where)?
y-m-14-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you give a figure different from the equilateral triangle and the regular pentagon?
y-m-14-05.s.s3.model.0: An isosceles triangle (a triangle with two sides of equal length) fits on both sides if you fold it from the vertex to the middle of the base, so it is line symmetric. But when turned half a turn the vertex goes to the bottom and it does not fit the original shape, so it is not point symmetric.
y-m-14-05.s.s3.model.1: An isosceles trapezoid whose bottom side is longer than its top side fits when folded through the middle of left and right. But when turned half a turn the long side goes to the top and it does not fit the original figure, so it is not a point-symmetric figure.
y-m-14-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: I can explain the same way with another figure too.

y-m-14-06.title: How many kinds of rectangular-prism frames can you make with 60 cm of wire?
y-m-14-06.topic: Rectangular prism: sum of edge lengths and designing the shape
y-m-14-06.goal: Express the condition on the sum of edge lengths as an equation, find without omission all the rectangular-prism frames that satisfy several conditions, and explain that there may be no frame when the conditions change.
y-m-14-06.material: You want to use all 60 cm of wire, with none left over, to make a frame (a skeleton with no faces) made only of the edges of a rectangular prism. The wire can be cut and joined, but you must not leave a single piece unused or overlap any. The length, width, and height are all natural numbers (cm). The longest edge of the frame must be at least 9 cm, and the shortest edge must be at least 2 cm.
y-m-14-06.thinking.0: Turning the structure of the 12 edges into an equation
y-m-14-06.thinking.1: Systematically finding different solutions within the conditions
y-m-14-06.thinking.2: Judging that there may be no solution when the conditions change
y-m-14-06.prereq.0: Knowing the edges, vertices, and faces of a rectangular prism
y-m-14-06.prereq.1: Knowing that opposite edges of a rectangular prism have equal lengths
y-m-14-06.s.s1.prompt: Which one correctly expresses, in terms of the length, width, and height, the condition of using all 60 cm of wire with none left over?
y-m-14-06.s.s1.hint.0: Picture a rectangular box, count its edges, and group the edges that have the same length.
y-m-14-06.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many edges correspond to the length.
y-m-14-06.s.s1.r.a: This idea counted only three of the 12 edges as wire. Count how many edges a rectangular-prism frame has.
y-m-14-06.s.s1.r.b: This idea counted the edges by grouping those with the same length.
y-m-14-06.s.s1.r.c: This idea counted all 12 edges as the sum of three lengths. Check how many edges there are of each same length.
y-m-14-06.s.s1.r.d: This idea counted the length of the wire like a volume. What the wire is used for is the lengths of the edges.
y-m-14-06.s.s1.explain: A rectangular prism has 12 edges, with 4 edges each corresponding to the length, width, and height. So the length of the wire is (length+width+height)×4, and if this is 60, then length+width+height=15.
y-m-14-06.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different frames that satisfy all the conditions. Choose the length a, width b, and height c. (Swapping a, b, c counts as the same frame.)
y-m-14-06.s.s2.hint.0: First decide what the sum of the three lengths must be, then choose one longest edge and fit the other two lengths.
y-m-14-06.s.s2.hint.1: At the end, check whether the shortest edge is at least 2 cm and whether the longest edge is at least 9 cm.
y-m-14-06.s.s2.ok.c1: All three lengths are natural numbers.
y-m-14-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The length, width, and height must be natural numbers (cm).
y-m-14-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The shortest edge is at least 2 cm.
y-m-14-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The shortest edge is shorter than 2 cm.
y-m-14-06.s.s2.ok.c3: The longest edge is at least 9 cm.
y-m-14-06.s.s2.fail.c3: The longest edge is shorter than 9 cm.
y-m-14-06.s.s2.ok.c4: It uses all 60 cm of wire with none left over.
y-m-14-06.s.s2.fail.c4: The sum of the edge lengths is not 60 cm. Check the sum of the 12 edges again.
y-m-14-06.s.s2.explain: The frames that satisfy the conditions are the four (9, 4, 2), (9, 3, 3), (10, 3, 2), and (11, 2, 2) (swapping the three lengths gives the same frame). For example, (9, 4, 2) gives 4×(9+4+2)=60 cm.
y-m-14-06.s.s2.because.prompt: How did you check that the number of frames you found is enough (or how could you check)? Explain the way you search.
y-m-14-06.s.s2.because.hint.0: Decide the longest edge in order starting from 9 cm, and write what the sum of the other two lengths must be.
y-m-14-06.s.s2.because.hint.1: For each case you decide, write down all the ways to split the other two lengths so that both are at least 2 cm.
y-m-14-06.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g. The sum of the three lengths is ..., so I fix the longest edge starting from ... and ...
y-m-14-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Can you say that no frame was missed with the method you wrote?
y-m-14-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Is it clear where you used the condition that the sum is 15?
y-m-14-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you check that (10, 3, 2) and (3, 10, 2) are counted as the same frame?
y-m-14-06.s.s2.because.model.0: The sum of the three lengths must be 15, so I fixed the longest edge one at a time as 9, 10, 11, 12, and looked for cases where the sum of the other two lengths is 6, 5, 4, 3. For 12 the sum is 3, so both cannot be at least 2, and there is none.
y-m-14-06.s.s2.because.model.1: I made a table and worked it out by splitting into cases: when the longest edge is 9, when it is 10, and so on. The sum is 15, so if it is 9, the sum of the other two is 6, and they are 2 and 4 or 3 and 3.
y-m-14-06.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: This is the method of splitting into cases with a table.
y-m-14-06.s.s3.prompt: The conditions have changed. The shortest edge is still at least 2 cm, and the longest edge must be at least 12 cm. The wire is still 60 cm, used with none left over. What can you say about the frame in this case?
y-m-14-06.s.s3.hint.0: Use the fact that the sum of the three lengths is 15, and find the sum of the other two lengths when the longest edge is 12.
y-m-14-06.s.s3.hint.1: Compare what the sum must be at minimum for both of the other two lengths to be at least 2 cm.
y-m-14-06.s.s3.o.a: It can be made. For example, make a frame with length 12 cm, width 2 cm, and height 1 cm.
y-m-14-06.s.s3.r.a: You left out one condition. All edges must be at least 2 cm. Also check the sum again.
y-m-14-06.s.s3.o.b: It can be made. For example, make a frame with length 12 cm, width 3 cm, and height 3 cm.
y-m-14-06.s.s3.r.b: You did not check what the sum of the three lengths must be.
y-m-14-06.s.s3.o.c: It can't be made. If you use 12 cm, the sum of the other two lengths is 3, so both cannot be at least 2 cm.
y-m-14-06.s.s3.r.c: This choice was made by using the condition on the sum and examining the remaining two lengths.
y-m-14-06.s.s3.o.d: We can't tell. We can't say anything until we actually try making a frame with a 12 cm edge.
y-m-14-06.s.s3.r.d: Trying it out is also a way, but the sum is fixed at 15, so you can judge by reasoning.
y-m-14-06.s.s3.explain: The sum of the three lengths is 15. If the longest edge is 12 or more, the sum of the other two lengths is 3 or less, but for both to be at least 2 cm the sum must be at least 4. So there is no frame that satisfies all the conditions. When you change the conditions, you need to check that 'there may be no solution'.

y-m-14-07.title: A solution for how many tiles to lay: where does it go wrong?
y-m-14-07.topic: Units of area: converting between m² and cm², and laying tiles
y-m-14-07.goal: Find and fix the error made when converting between m² and cm², find in several ways the conditions under which tiles can be laid without cutting and without gaps, and judge whether it is possible when the conditions change.
y-m-14-07.material: You want to cover the classroom floor with square tiles that are 40 cm on each side. The classroom floor is a rectangle 6 m long and 4 m wide. The tiles are not cut, and they cover the whole floor with no gaps or overlaps. (1 m = 100 cm)
y-m-14-07.thinking.0: Finding an error in converting units
y-m-14-07.thinking.1: Finding several solutions that fit the conditions
y-m-14-07.thinking.2: Comparing two reasons why something is not possible
y-m-14-07.prereq.1: Knowing the area of a rectangle
y-m-14-07.s.s1.prompt: Yunseo found the number of tiles needed like this. Pick the first line that goes wrong.
y-m-14-07.s.s1.hint.0: Next to each line, write whether the unit used is m, m², cm, or cm².
y-m-14-07.s.s1.hint.1: Convert a square with 1 m sides into cm, and find its area in cm² directly.
y-m-14-07.s.s1.line.0: The area of the floor is 6×4=24 m².
y-m-14-07.s.s1.line.1: The area of one tile is 40×40=1600 cm².
y-m-14-07.s.s1.line.2: 1 m is 100 cm, so 24 m² is 2400 cm².
y-m-14-07.s.s1.line.3: The number of tiles is 2400÷1600=1.5, so 2 tiles are enough.
y-m-14-07.s.s1.explain: Line 3 goes wrong. Since 1 m=100 cm, 1 m² is a square 100 cm by 100 cm, so it is 100×100=10000 cm². Then 24 m² is 240000 cm², and 240000÷1600=150 tiles. Compared with the fact that even one row needs 15 tiles, '2 tiles' in line 4 makes no sense.
y-m-14-07.s.s2.prompt: Choose the side of a square tile that can cover the 6 m by 4 m floor with no gaps and without cutting the tiles. The side must be a natural number (cm) from 10 cm to 100 cm. Find 3 different sizes.
y-m-14-07.s.s2.hint.0: Decide on one side length for the tile, and check whether the tiles fit exactly across the 600 cm in the length direction.
y-m-14-07.s.s2.hint.1: Even if a size fits along the length, separately check whether there is some left over or short along the 400 cm width.
y-m-14-07.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a natural number from 10 cm to 100 cm.
y-m-14-07.s.s2.fail.c1: The side of the tile must be a natural number (cm) from 10 cm to 100 cm.
y-m-14-07.s.s2.ok.c2: It covers the 600 cm length with no gaps.
y-m-14-07.s.s2.fail.c2: Along the 600 cm length, tiles are left over or short.
y-m-14-07.s.s2.ok.c3: It covers the 400 cm width with no gaps.
y-m-14-07.s.s2.fail.c3: Along the 400 cm width, tiles are left over or short.
y-m-14-07.s.s2.explain: From 10 cm to 100 cm, the sizes that work are the six sizes 10, 20, 25, 40, 50, and 100 cm. For example, with 50 cm, 12 tiles fit along the length and 8 along the width, so 96 tiles are needed. With 30 cm or 60 cm the length works, but along the 400 cm width they do not fit exactly.
y-m-14-07.s.s3.prompt: The room has changed to 6 m long and 4.5 m wide. You want to judge that the floor cannot be covered with no gaps when the same 40 cm tiles are used without cutting. Choose all the appropriate reasons for this judgment.
y-m-14-07.s.s3.hint.0: Write which numbers must be natural numbers in the method using area and in the method using length.
y-m-14-07.s.s3.hint.1: Convert 6 m to 600 cm and 4.5 m to 450 cm, and see how many tiles fit in each direction.
y-m-14-07.s.s3.o.a: If you divide the area 27 m²=270000 cm² by the tile's 1600 cm², you get 168.75 tiles, which is not a natural number
y-m-14-07.s.s3.r.a: This idea was judged by the condition that the number of tiles must be a natural number.
y-m-14-07.s.s3.o.b: 4.5 m is not a natural number, so even after converting to cm we cannot count how many tiles fit in one row
y-m-14-07.s.s3.r.b: This judgment said tiles cannot be laid just because a decimal appeared. 450 cm is a natural-number length.
y-m-14-07.s.s3.o.c: If you lay tiles in one row along the 450 cm width, 11 tiles fit and 10 cm is left over, so it cannot be covered without cutting
y-m-14-07.s.s3.r.c: This idea checked the condition using the length in one direction.
y-m-14-07.s.s3.o.d: The room got bigger, so if more tiles are used, the problem of sizes not fitting disappears, and it can be covered without cutting
y-m-14-07.s.s3.r.d: This idea took it that using more tiles makes the problem of sizes not fitting go away. The problem is not the number of tiles but whether the lengths fit exactly.
y-m-14-07.s.s3.explain: By area, 270000÷1600=168.75, and by length, 450÷40=11.25, so both support the judgment that it cannot be covered without gaps unless the tiles are cut. The fact that 4.5 m is a decimal or that the number of tiles is increased is not a reason.

y-m-14-08.title: If you estimate a leaf's area with a grid, how far can you go in what you say?
y-m-14-08.topic: Estimating area: finding a range with a grid
y-m-14-08.goal: Express the area of a curved shape as a range using the number of grid squares, adjust your confidence depending on how the range changes when the grid is made smaller, and explain how to report an estimate.
y-m-14-08.material: You placed a leaf on grid paper in which each square is 1 cm wide and 1 cm tall, and traced around its outline. The area of one grid square is 1 cm². Hyunwoo wants to estimate the area of this leaf drawing. The outline is curved, so it does not fit the squares exactly.
y-m-14-08.thinking.0: Expressing an estimate as a range
y-m-14-08.thinking.1: Adjusting your judgment and confidence according to new information
y-m-14-08.thinking.2: Telling an exact value from an estimate
y-m-14-08.prereq.0: Knowing the unit of area, cm²
y-m-14-08.prereq.1: Estimating area using the area of one grid square and the number of squares
y-m-14-08.s.s1.prompt: Each time you receive information, choose what you can say about the area of the leaf drawing, and revise your judgment and confidence.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.hint.0: From the information received so far, write down separately the smallest and the largest values the area could be.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the new information falls inside the earlier range or goes outside it.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.info: When you counted the grid, there were 14 squares fully inside the leaf drawing and 12 squares that the outline passes through, so only part of them is inside. The remaining squares do not overlap the leaf.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.ask: What can you say about the area of the leaf drawing from this information?
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.after: The squares fully inside are all within the leaf, so the area is at least 14 cm². Even if all the squares the outline passes through were completely full, it could not exceed 26 cm². So you can say it is at least 14 cm² and at most 26 cm², but this information does not tell you which value in between it is.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The area is exactly 20 cm². This is because it is the value counting the 12 partly-inside squares as half each.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Counting half for each is one way to estimate. It is not guaranteed to be the exact value.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.o.b: The area is at least 14 cm² and at most 26 cm²
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This judgment set the smallest and largest values of the area using the squares fully inside and the squares the outline passes through.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The area is exactly 14 cm². This is because only the squares fully inside are counted and the squares the outline passes through are not counted.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This idea took the area of the partly-inside squares to be 0. There is leaf in those squares too.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.o.d: You can estimate it as about 20 cm², but you don't know where between 14 and 26 the exact value is
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This judgment used an estimate while also saying that it is not the exact value.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.o.e: Some squares are only partly crossed by the leaf, so the area could be bigger than 26 cm²
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.0.r.e: Even when the 12 squares the outline passes through are as large as possible, the total is 26 cm². Squares outside the leaf do not count toward the area.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.info: To find out more precisely, Hyunwoo changed the grid to squares with sides of 0.5 cm and counted again. The area of one square is 0.25 cm². There were 66 squares fully inside and 20 squares only partly inside.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.ask: With this new information, what can you say now about the area of the leaf drawing?
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.after: When you count again with the smaller squares, the smallest value is 66×0.25=16.5 cm² and the largest value is (66+20)×0.25=21.5 cm². The width of the range shrank from 12 cm² to 5 cm². The new range lies inside the earlier range of 14 to 26, so the earlier judgment was not wrong, and the estimate 'about 20 cm²' is also inside the new range.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The area is at least 16.5 cm² and at most 21.5 cm², and 'about 20 cm²' is also inside this
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This judgment saw that the range became narrower with the new information, and checked whether the earlier estimate is inside the new range.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It has newly turned out that the earlier statement 'at least 14 cm² and at most 26 cm²' was wrong
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This idea took the earlier range and the new range to contradict each other. The new range is inside the earlier range.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The area has been fixed at exactly 19 cm². This is because it is exactly the middle value of 16.5 and 21.5
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This idea took the middle value to be the exact value. There are still 20 partly-inside squares.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Even though the squares got smaller, there are partly-inside squares, so the range of the estimate has become wider
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This judgment was made without calculating how the width of the range changed. Compare the widths of the earlier range and the new range.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.2.info: Mina counted the partly-inside squares as half each. With 0.5 cm squares it is 66+20÷2=76 squares, and she said 76×0.25=19 cm².
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.2.ask: How should we view the 19 cm² that Mina found?
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.2.after: 19 cm² lies between 16.5 cm² and 21.5 cm², so it does not contradict the earlier result. Counting half each is an estimate that assumes the squares the outline passes through are on average about half full, so you cannot claim it is the exact value.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It is the exact area. This is because the method of counting half each always gives the exact value.
y-m-14-08.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This idea took the value counted by halves to be the exact value.
